text: A state vector that only ever gets printed as raw numbers isn't very useful to a human reader. This lesson adds the two things that make the toolkit actually interpretable: computing real measurement probabilities and sampling outcomes from them, and plotting the result.

probabilities takes abs of each amplitude squared, for every basis state. Reproducible sampling draws from that distribution with a seeded random number generator, and gets checked against exact, deterministically computable expected counts rather than one specific random draw. bloch_coordinates maps a single qubit's alpha and beta amplitudes to an x, y, z point. And both the measurement histogram and the Bloch vector get plotted with Matplotlib, checked against the same confirmed numbers, not separately invented examples.

Running probabilities on the Bell state from last lesson, point seven zero seven one, zero, zero, point seven zero seven one, gives back point five, zero, zero, point five. Zero point seven zero seven one squared rounds to exactly point five, confirming equal fifty percent chances of ket-zero-zero or ket-one-one, and zero chance of the other two — the numerical signature of entanglement.

For the plus state, alpha equals beta equals one over root two, x equals two real of alpha times the conjugate of beta works out to one, y works out to zero since there are no imaginary parts anywhere, and z works out to zero. That lands at one, zero, zero, the plus state sitting exactly on the Bloch sphere's equator along the x-axis, matching the known fact that plus is the equal real superposition of zero and one.

The toolkit runs, but that's not the same question as whether it's correct, tested, and something another person could pick up and trust. Next lesson is a real code review of everything built in Lessons 22 through 24.
